4104.stem: A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ where $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.latex: Explain why the particle never changes direction.
Find the displacement $x$ of the particle after 1 second.
For sufficiently large values of $t$ (as $t\to\infty$), describe the behaviour of the displacement of the particle.
Find the exact acceleration of the particle at $t=4$ seconds.

solutions.latex:
The range of $v=2-2\sin(2\pi t)$ is $[0,4]$.

So $v\ge 0$ for all $t$.

Therefore the particle is only ever stationary or travelling in the positive direction, so it never changes direction.

Integrate the velocity.
$$x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=0+\dfrac{1}{\pi}+C \\ C&=-\dfrac{1}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
So $x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)-\dfrac{1}{\pi}$.

When $t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2+\dfrac{1}{\pi}-\dfrac{1}{\pi} \\ &=2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

$$x=2t+\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(2\pi t)-\dfrac{1}{\pi}$$
The cosine term is bounded, so as $t\to\infty$, $x\to\infty$.

Therefore the displacement approaches infinity.

Students can also use the fact that the particle never changes direction from part (a).

Differentiate the velocity.
$$a=-4\pi\cos(2\pi t)$$
When $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-4\pi\cos(8\pi) \\ &=-4\pi \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct acceleration equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right)=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}$.
Hence find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dx}{9-x^2}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule inside the logarithm, with $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)\right]&=\dfrac{\frac{(3-x)(1)-(3+x)(-1)}{(3-x)^2}}{\frac{3+x}{3-x}} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{(3-x)^2}\cdot\dfrac{3-x}{3+x} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{(3-x)(3+x)} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, using log laws:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(3+x)-\ln(3-x)\right]&=\dfrac{1}{3+x}+\dfrac{1}{3-x} \\ &=\dfrac{(3-x)+(3+x)}{(3+x)(3-x)} \\ &=\dfrac{6}{9-x^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the differentiation rule, or equivalent merit
Uses the quotient rule or log laws, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: The source quotient-rule line has been formatted as given; criteria wording mentions integration though the part is differentiation, kept in spirit.

solutions.latex:
From part (a):
$$\int\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx=\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)+C$$
Divide by 6.
$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{1}{9-x^2}\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{6}\int\dfrac{6}{9-x^2}\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{6}\ln\left(\dfrac{3+x}{3-x}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$

4107.stem: The first term of a geometric series is $e^{x}$ and the fifth term is $81e^{9x}$.

parts.latex: Show that the common ratio can be expressed by $r=3e^{2x}$.
Find an expression for the $8^{\text{th}}$ term of the series.
For what values of $x$ does the series have a limiting sum?
Find the exact value of $x$ if the limiting sum is 3.

solutions.latex:
For a geometric series, $T_n=ar^{n-1}$, with $a=e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_5=e^x r^4&=81e^{9x} \\ r^4&=81e^{8x} \\ r&=\sqrt[4]{81e^{8x}} \\ &=3e^{2x} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
A limiting sum exists when $|r|<1$.
$$|3e^{2x}|<1$$
Since $3e^{2x}>0$ for all $x$, this becomes:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&<3e^{2x}<1 \\ 0&<e^{2x}<\dfrac{1}{3} &&(\text{divide by } 3) \\ 2x&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) &&(\text{take } \ln) \\ x&<\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) &&(\text{divide by } 2) \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Use $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=\dfrac{e^x}{1-3e^{2x}} \\ 3\left(1-3e^{2x}\right)&=e^x \\ 3-9e^{2x}&=e^x \\ 0&=9e^{2x}+e^x-3 \end{aligned}$$
Let $u=e^x$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=9u^2+u-3 \\ u&=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{1-4(9)(-3)}}{18} \\ &=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{109}}{18} \end{aligned}$$
Since $u=e^x>0$, $u$ cannot be negative.
$$e^x=\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{109}}{18}$$
$$\therefore\ x=\ln\left(\dfrac{-1+\sqrt{109}}{18}\right)\approx-0.65$$

A factory located next to a lake has recently been shut down due to concerns about chemical run off. A bird's eye view of the lake is given in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1305_q5_1}

Local volunteers have begun a clean-up effort to remove these harmful chemicals from the lake. The concentration of chemicals is given by the equation:

$$C=1.5-0.4e^{kt}$$

Let $C$ be the concentration of chemicals in the lake in kg/m$^3$, where $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the number of years after the clean-up effort has started.

figures.cap: bird's eye view of lake with five widths 45, 80, 90, 60, 55 m at 25 m spacing

parts.latex: The initial weight of chemical run off in the lake is 38500 kg, and the average depth of the lake is 5 m. Use the trapezoidal rule to show that the initial concentration of chemical run off can be estimated as 1.1 kg/m$^3$.
Find the value of $k$ to three significant figures if it takes 2.45 years to remove all chemical run off from the lake
Find the rate of change in the concentration of chemical run off in the lake at $t=1.8$ years. Round your answer to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Trapezoidal rule with width $h=25$ and the measured widths from the diagram:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\dfrac{25}{2}\left(45+55+2(80+90+60)\right) \\ &=7000 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Volume $=$ area $\times$ depth:
$$V=7000\times 5=35000 \text{ m}^3$$
Concentration is weight divided by volume:
$$\dfrac{38500 \text{ kg}}{35000 \text{ m}^3}=1.1 \text{ kg/m}^3$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule and finds the volume, or equivalent merit
Applies the trapezoidal rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
All chemical is removed when $C=0$ at $t=2.45$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=1.5-0.4e^{2.45k} \\ \dfrac{1.5}{0.4}&=e^{2.45k} \\ 2.45k&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1.5}{0.4}\right) \\ k&=\dfrac{\ln(1.5\div 0.4)}{2.45} \\ &=0.539 \text{ (3 significant figures)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Working towards correct answer, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $C=1.5-0.4e^{0.539t}$.
$$\dfrac{dC}{dt}=-0.4\times 0.539\,e^{0.539t}$$
When $t=1.8$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dC}{dt}&=-0.4\times 0.539\,e^{0.539\times 1.8} \\ &=-0.5699\ldots \\ &\approx -0.57 \text{ kg/m}^3 \text{ per year} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Working towards correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the position of particle $P$ is given by $x=(t-2)^2+4$.
Explain why particles $P$ and $Q$ will never collide.
Show that the distance between the particles can be given by $PQ=(t-2)^2+\ln(t+1)$.
Find the exact time that the distance between the particles $PQ$ is a minimum.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity.
$$x=t^2-4t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=8$, so $C=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=t^2-4t+8 \\ &=(t-2)^2+4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates correctly and finds $C$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: The displacement-time graphs of $P$ and $Q$ never intersect, so the particles are never at the same position and never collide.
$$\begin{aligned} PQ&=\left((t-2)^2+4\right)-\left(4-\ln(t+1)\right) \\ &=(t-2)^2+4-4+\ln(t+1) \\ &=(t-2)^2+\ln(t+1) \end{aligned}$$

Stationary values occur where $PQ'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} PQ'&=2(t-2)+\dfrac{1}{t+1}=0 \\ 2t-4&=-\dfrac{1}{t+1} \\ (2t-4)(t+1)&=-1 \\ 2t^2-2t-4+1&=0 \\ 2t^2-2t-3&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Solve using the quadratic formula.
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-4(2)(-3)}}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{28}}{4} \\ &=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{7}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Since $t\ge 0$, $t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}$.

Test the nature with the second derivative.
$$PQ''=2-\dfrac{1}{(1+t)^2}$$
At $t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}$:
$$PQ''=2-\dfrac{1}{\left(1+\frac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2}\right)^2}\approx 1.8757>0$$
So the stationary point is a minimum.
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{7}}{2} \text{ s}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly and expresses as a quadratic, or equivalent merit

The sector angles sum to the full circle, so $S_{12}=360$. The largest angle is twice the smallest, so $T_{12}=2T_1=2a$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:
$$\begin{aligned}360&=\dfrac{12}{2}(a+2a) \\ 60&=3a \\ a&=20\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)=2$, show that $x^2-3x-4=0$.
Hence, find the solution(s) of the equation $\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)=2$.

solutions.latex:
Combine the logarithms using $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$.
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)&=2 \\ \log_2\big(x(x-3)\big)&=2 \\ x(x-3)&=2^2 \\ x^2-3x-4&=0\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies a log law correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-3x-4&=0 \\ (x-4)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=4$ or $x=-1$.

The logarithms need $x>0$ and $x-3>0$, so $x>3$.

Hence $-1$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x=4$$

meta.format_note: Source factorised as $(x-4)(x-1)$ giving $x=1$; correct factors are $(x-4)(x+1)$ giving $x=-1$. Fixed; conclusion $x=4$ unchanged.

figures.cap: rectangle OABC with sectors OAP and OCQ

parts.latex: Find the exact arc length $CQ$.
Find the exact area of the sector $OAP$.
Find the exact length of interval $AP$, correct to 1 decimal place.

solutions.latex:
Angles at $O$ on a straight line sum to $\pi$; $\angle AOC=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (rectangle) and $\angle AOP=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle COQ&=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The radius of arc $CQ$ is $OC=2$ cm, so using $l=r\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}l_{CQ}&=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$

The radius of sector $OAP$ is $OA=7$ cm. Using $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 7^2\times\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{49\pi}{12}\text{ cm}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the formula correctly (recognising the radius), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Apply the cosine rule in triangle $OAP$, where $OP=OA=7$ cm.
$$\begin{aligned}AP^2&=OP^2+OA^2-2\times OP\times OA\cos\angle AOP \\ &=7^2+7^2-2\times 7\times 7\times\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=98-98\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=98-49\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
So
$$\begin{aligned}AP&=\sqrt{98-49\sqrt{3}} \\ &\approx 3.6234\ldots \\ &\approx 3.6\text{ cm (1 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the cosine rule correctly, or equivalent merit

4129.stem: The probability that a student plays badminton is 0.3. The probability that a student plays neither table tennis or badminton is 0.5, and the probability that a student plays both sports is $x$.

figures.cap: Venn diagram with B, T and 0.5 outside

parts.latex:
Using the Venn diagram, or otherwise, complete the probabilities below.

\exfigure{1306_q18_1}

$P(B)=\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$

$P(B\cap T)=\_\_\_\_$
Find the probability that a student plays table tennis but not badminton

It is known that if a student plays table tennis, the probability that they also play badminton is 0.5

Find the probability that a student plays both badminton and table tennis.
Hence, or otherwise, determine the probability that a student plays only badminton.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities in the Venn diagram sum to $1$.
$$\begin{aligned}1&=0.5+P(B)+P(T)-P(B\cap T) \\ 0.5&=0.3+P(T)-x \\ P(T)&=0.2+x\end{aligned}$$
Table tennis but not badminton:
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(T\cap\overline{B}\right)&=P(T)-P(B\cap T) \\ &=0.2+x-x \\ &=0.2\end{aligned}$$

Using the conditional probability formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P(B\mid T)&=\dfrac{P(B\cap T)}{P(T)} \\ 0.5&=\dfrac{x}{0.2+x} \\ 0.1+0.5x&=x \\ 0.1&=0.5x \\ x&=0.2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(B\cap T)=0.2$$
criteria: Applies the conditional probability formula and substitutes, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Badminton only is badminton less both sports.
$$\begin{aligned}P\left(B\cap\overline{T}\right)&=0.3-x \\ &=0.3-0.2 \\ &=0.1\end{aligned}$$

4131.stem:
A particle moves such that its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, at a time $t$ seconds is given by $\dot{x}=4-8\cos t$.

The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.latex: Find the two times the particle is first at rest?
Find the equation for displacement $x$ in terms of time $t$.
Find the exact distance travelled by the particle between the first two times it is at rest.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4-8\cos t \\ 8\cos t&=4 \\ \cos t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The first quadrant solution is $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is also positive in the fourth quadrant:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\end{aligned}$$
The first two times the particle is at rest are $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ seconds and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ seconds.
criteria: Reaches $\cos t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and the first quadrant solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrating the velocity gives the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int(4-8\cos t)\,dt\\&=4t-8\sin t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle is at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4(0)-8\sin 0+C\\C&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=4t-8\sin t$$

The particle is at rest when $4-8\cos t=0$, that is $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$. Since $v>0$ between these times, the distance travelled is the difference in displacement.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=4\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}-8\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-8\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
When $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=4\times\dfrac{5\pi}{3}-8\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\\&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+8\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\dfrac{20\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}-\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-4\sqrt{3}\right)\\&=\dfrac{16\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}\text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one correct displacement for one of the times, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rest times from part (a) and the sign of $v$ added as brief set-up, not in source.

4132.stem: The population of an island is increasing according to the formula $P=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}$ where $P$ is the population in thousands and $t$ is the time in years after January 1st 2020.

parts.latex: Find the initial rate of change of the population of the island.
Use the model to predict the population on 1st January 2040, correct to the nearest thousand.
Using the model, predict in what year will the population reach 40 000.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating the population formula:
$$\begin{aligned}P&=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=10\times\dfrac{1}{50}e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}e^{\frac{t}{50}}\end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{5}e^0=\dfrac{1}{5}$$
$P$ is in thousands, so initially the population is increasing at a rate of $200$ people per year.

On 1 January 2040, $t=20$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=20+10e^{\frac{20}{50}}\\&\approx 34.9182\end{aligned}$$
The predicted population on 1 January 2040 is $35\,000$.

The population is $40$ thousand, so $P=40$.
$$\begin{aligned}40&=20+10e^{\frac{t}{50}}\\e^{\frac{t}{50}}&=2\\\dfrac{t}{50}&=\ln 2\\t&=50\ln 2\\&\approx 34.657\end{aligned}$$
The population will reach $40\,000$ during 2054.
criteria: Substitutes and starts solving the equation, or equivalent merit

4133.stem:
The height of water $h$ metres in a harbour can be modelled using the function below:

$h=4-A\sin(bt)$, where $t$ is the time in hours after midnight.

\exfigure{1306_q22_1}

At 2 am the height of water in the harbour is at its minimum.

At 6 am the height of water in the harbour is at its maximum.

figures.cap: graph of h against t, minimum 2 at t=2, maximum 6 at t=6, period 8

parts.latex: Find the values of $A$ and $b$.

A boat can only enter the harbour when the height of the water is more than 5 metres.

Express the information given as an equation, and solve the equation to find the first time the boat can enter the harbour.

solutions.latex:
The minimum is at 2 am and the maximum at 6 am, so the minimum height is $2$ and the maximum is $6$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{amplitude}&=\dfrac{6-2}{2}\\&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A=2$$
Half a period is $4$ hours (from minimum to maximum), so the period is $8$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{2\pi}{b}&=8\\b&=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore A=2,\ b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$
criteria: At least one correct value, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The boat can enter when $h>5$, so first solve $h=5$ with $A=2$, $b=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned}5&=4-2\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\\\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\pi t}{4}&=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\&=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\\t&=\dfrac{28}{6},\ \dfrac{44}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The first time is $t=\dfrac{28}{6}=4\text{ h }40\text{ min}$.
$$\therefore\text{ the boat can first enter at } 4{:}40 \text{ am}$$
criteria: Sets up the equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with 4 sub-intervals to estimate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{x}\,dx$, correct to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
There are 4 sub-intervals on $[0,2]$, so $h=\dfrac{2-0}{4}=0.5$ and the $x$ values are $0,\ 0.5,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 2$.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^2\sqrt{x}\,dx&\approx\dfrac{0.5}{2}\left(\sqrt{0}+\sqrt{2}+2\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}}+\sqrt{1}+\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)\right)\\&\approx 1.8194\\&\approx 1.82\text{ (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the table or substitutes correctly into the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that the equation $2\cos^2 x=4-5\sin x$ may be written as $2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2=0$.
Hence solve $2\cos^2 x=4-5\sin x$, for $0^\circ\le x\le 360^\circ$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\cos^2 x=1-\sin^2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2 x&=4-5\sin x\\2\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)&=4-5\sin x\\2-2\sin^2 x&=4-5\sin x\\2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+4-2&=0\\2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2&=0\end{aligned}$$

From part (a), the equation is $2\sin^2 x-5\sin x+2=0$. Factorise.
$$\begin{aligned}2\sin^2 x-4\sin x-\sin x+2&=0\\2\sin x(\sin x-2)-1(\sin x-2)&=0\\(2\sin x-1)(\sin x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\sin x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\sin x=2$.

Since $-1\le\sin x\le 1$, $\sin x=2$ is rejected.
$$\sin x=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ x=30^\circ,\ 150^\circ$$
criteria: Finds the quadratic in terms of $\sin x$ and factorises, or equivalent merit

4136.stem: The line $y=24(x-1)$ is tangent to the curve $y=ax^3+bx^2+4$ at $x=2$.

parts.latex: Using the fact that the tangent meets the curve to show that $2a+b=5$.
By finding another relationship between $a$ and $b$, find the values of $a$ and $b$.

solutions.latex:
When $x=2$ the tangent has
$$\begin{aligned}y&=24(2-1)\\&=24\end{aligned}$$
The point of contact is $(2,24)$, which also lies on the curve $y=ax^3+bx^2+4$.
$$\begin{aligned}24&=a\times 2^3+b\times 2^2+4\\24&=8a+4b+4\\20&=8a+4b\\5&=2a+b\quad\ldots(1)\end{aligned}$$

The gradient of the curve at $x=2$ equals the gradient of the tangent, $24$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=3ax^2+2bx\\24&=3a\times 2^2+2b\times 2\\24&=12a+4b\\6&=3a+b\quad\ldots(2)\end{aligned}$$
Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$a=1$$
Substituting into (1): $2+b=5$.
$$\therefore\ a=1,\ b=3$$
criteria: Differentiates and sets the gradient equal to $24$, or equivalent merit

4137.stem:
Two children, Jack and Jill, each throw two fair cubical dice simultaneously.

The score for each child is the sum of the two numbers shown on their respective dice.

figures.cap: blank 6 by 6 table for the sum of two dice
partial tree diagram for Die 1 to Die 4 with branches 1,2 and 3,4,5,6
partly completed probability distribution table for X

parts.latex:
Complete the table below for the sum of two fair cubical dice below.

\exfigure{1306_q26_1}
Calculate the probability that Jack obtains a score of 9.
Calculate the probability that Jack and Jill each obtain a score of 9.
By considering the symmetry of the table in (a), show that the probability of Jack and Jill obtaining the same score is $\dfrac{73}{648}$.
Find the probability that Jack's score exceeds Jill's score.
Calculate $E(X)$, correct to 2 decimal places.
Find $\text{Var}(X)$, correct to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex: \extable{Ts6024_1}

There are $4$ ways of scoring $9$ out of $36$ equally likely outcomes.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Jack gets }9)&=\dfrac{4}{36}\\&=\dfrac{1}{9}\end{aligned}$$

The two children throw independently, so the probabilities multiply.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Jack and Jill both score }9)&=P(\text{Jack scores }9)\times P(\text{Jill scores }9)\\&=\dfrac{1}{9}\times\dfrac{1}{9}\\&=\dfrac{1}{81}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had an ampersand inside \text; replaced with 'and' to avoid a LaTeX alignment error.

solutions.latex:
By symmetry of the table, $P(k,k)$ for score $k$ equals $P(14-k,14-k)$, so the scores $2$ to $6$ are matched with $12$ to $8$.
$$\begin{aligned}&P(\text{same score})\\&=P(2,2)+P(3,3)+\cdots+P(12,12)\\&=2P(2,2)+2P(3,3)+2P(4,4)+2P(5,5)+2P(6,6)+P(7,7)\\&=P(7,7)+2\big[P(2,2)+P(3,3)+P(4,4)+P(5,5)+P(6,6)\big]\\&=\left(\dfrac{6}{36}\right)^2+2\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{2}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{4}{36}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{5}{36}\right)^2\right]\\&=\dfrac{73}{648}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to work towards the probability, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's middle line used an ellipsis-free full sum; shortened with $\cdots$ in the first expansion only. Symmetry sentence added.

solutions.latex:
The events Jack scores more, less, or the same as Jill are exhaustive. By symmetry, $P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})=P(\text{Jack}<\text{Jill})$, and from part (d) $P(\text{Jack}=\text{Jill})=\dfrac{73}{648}$.
$$\begin{aligned}1&=P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})+P(\text{Jack}<\text{Jill})+P(\text{Jack}=\text{Jill})\\1&=2P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})+\dfrac{73}{648}\\2P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})&=1-\dfrac{73}{648}\\P(\text{Jack}>\text{Jill})&=\dfrac{575}{1296}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the equation, or uses the previous part to attempt the probability, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$X\le 2$ means every die shows $1$ or $2$. From the diagram, each die shows $1$ or $2$ with probability
$$P(1\text{ or }2\text{ on one die})=\dfrac{2}{6}$$
The four dice are independent.
$$\begin{aligned}P(1\text{ or }2\text{ on every die})&=\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{6}\times\dfrac{2}{6}\\&=\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^4\\&=\dfrac{1}{81}\end{aligned}$$
\extable{Ts6030_1}
criteria: Some correct values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $E(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$ with the distribution from part (g):
$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=1\times\dfrac{1}{1296}+2\times\dfrac{15}{1296}+3\times\dfrac{65}{1296}+4\times\dfrac{175}{1296}+5\times\dfrac{369}{1296}+6\times\dfrac{671}{1296}\\&\approx 5.24\text{ (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Values checked: $E(X)=\dfrac{6797}{1296}\approx 5.24$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\text{Var}(X)=E\left(X^2\right)-[E(X)]^2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Var}(X)&=E\left(X^2\right)-5.24^2\\&=\dfrac{1}{1296}+\dfrac{60}{1296}+\dfrac{585}{1296}+\dfrac{2800}{1296}+\dfrac{9225}{1296}+\dfrac{24156}{1296}-5.24^2\\&\approx 0.96\text{ (2 dp)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some correct working towards the variance, or equivalent merit

4138.stem:
The diagram shows a part of the curve with equation $x=y^2$ and a fixed point $S(1,0)$.

Point $P$ lies on the curve and has $y$-coordinate $k$, where $k\ge 0$.

\exfigure{1306_q27_1}

NOT TO SCALE

The distance of $P$ from the $y$-axis is $d$, and $r$ is the ratio $\dfrac{d}{SP}$

figures.cap: part of curve x=y^2, point S(1,0), point P and distance d to the y-axis

parts.latex: Show that $r=\dfrac{k^2}{\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}$
Show that $\dfrac{dr}{dk}=\dfrac{2k-k^3}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$.
By solving $\dfrac{dr}{dk}=0$, find and verify the value of $k$ that gives the maximum of $r$.
Hence, find the exact maximum value of $r$.

solutions.latex:
$P$ lies on $x=y^2$ with $y=k$, so $P\left(k^2,k\right)$.

The distance from the $y$-axis is the $x$-coordinate, so $d=k^2$.

Using the distance formula with $S(1,0)$:
$$\begin{aligned}PS^2&=\left(k^2-1\right)^2+(k-0)^2\\&=k^4-2k^2+1+k^2\\&=k^4-k^2+1\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{d}{PS}\\&=\dfrac{k^2}{\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Recognises the expression for $d$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dk}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned}u&=k^2 & v&=\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\u'&=2k & v'&=\dfrac{4k^3-2k}{2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}\end{aligned}$$
where $v'$ comes from the chain rule:
$$v'=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(4k^3-2k\right)$$
Substituting:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dr}{dk}&=\dfrac{\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\times 2k-k^2\times\frac{4k^3-2k}{2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}}{\left(\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\right)^2}\\&=\dfrac{4k\left(\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}\right)^2-k^2\left(4k^3-2k\right)}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)\times 2\sqrt{k^4-k^2+1}}\\&=\dfrac{4k\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)-k^2\left(4k^3-2k\right)}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{4k^5-4k^3+4k-4k^5+2k^3}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{4k-2k^3}{2\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\\&=\dfrac{2k-k^3}{\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For stationary points, set $\dfrac{dr}{dk}=0$. The denominator is never zero, so only the numerator matters.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4k\left(k^4-k^2+1\right)-k^2\left(4k^3-2k\right)\\0&=4k^5-4k^3+4k-4k^5+2k^3\\0&=4k-2k^3\\0&=2k\left(2-k^2\right)\end{aligned}$$
Since $k>0$:
$$k=\sqrt{2}$$
Test the sign of $\dfrac{dr}{dk}$ either side of $k=\sqrt{2}$:

\extable{Ts6035_1}

The gradient changes from positive to negative.
$$\therefore\ k=\sqrt{2}\text{ gives the maximum of } r$$
criteria: Solves the equation, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's first line set the numerator over the denominator equal to 0; reworded to numerator only (same mathematics).

solutions.latex:
Substitute $k=\sqrt{2}$ into $r$:
$$\begin{aligned}r&=\dfrac{\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^2}{\sqrt{\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^4-\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^2+1}}\\&=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{4-2+1}}\\&=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r_{\max}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$$

parts.latex:
Find the coordinates of any horizontal points of inflexion on the curve with equation

$y=x^4-8x^3+18x^2+4$

solutions.latex:
Differentiate twice.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^4-8x^3+18x^2+4\\\dfrac{dy}{dx}&=4x^3-24x^2+36x\\\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=12x^2-48x+36\end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflexion occur where $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=12x^2-48x+36\\0&=x^2-4x+3\\0&=(x-3)(x-1)\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=1\text{ or }x=3$$
For a horizontal point of inflexion, the value of $x$ must also be a stationary point, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$.

When $x=1$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(1)^3-24(1)^2+36(1)=16\ne 0$$
When $x=3$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=4(3)^3-24(3)^2+36(3)=0$$
So only $x=3$ is stationary. Check for a change of concavity:

\extable{Ts6037_1}

When $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=3^4-8(3)^3+18(3)^2+4\\&=31\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (3,31)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflexion}$$
criteria: Finds which value is also a stationary point and its $y$-value, or equivalent merit
Finds the values of $x$ that make the second derivative zero, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: parabola y=x^2 and line y=mx meeting at the origin and another point

parts.latex:
The area enclosed between the curve $y=x^2$ and the line $y=mx$ is $\dfrac{32}{3}$ square units.

\exfigure{1306_q29_1}

NOT TO SCALE

Find the value of $m$ if $m>0$.

solutions.latex:
Let the $x$-value of the point of intersection be $a$. The point lies on both $y=x^2$ and $y=mx$, so $a^2=ma$.
$$m=a$$
The line is above the curve between $x=0$ and $x=a$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{32}{3}&=\int_0^a\left(mx-x^2\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{mx^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^a\\&=\dfrac{ma^2}{2}-\dfrac{a^3}{3}\end{aligned}$$

When $x=1$:

A particular continuous random variable $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{32}, & 0\le x\le 8\\[4pt] 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

What is the median of this function?

solutions.latex:
The median $k$ satisfies $\displaystyle\int_0^k f(x)\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k\dfrac{x}{32}\,dx&=\left[\dfrac{x^2}{64}\right]_0^k \\ &=\dfrac{k^2}{64} \end{aligned}$$

Hence the answer is option B.

Differentiating:

For $x=-3$:

So there is a maximum at $(-3,0)$.

For $x=-1$:

So there is a minimum at $(-1,-4)$.

The total area is the circle plus the square, using $r=\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi}$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\pi r^2+x^2 \\ &=\pi\left(\dfrac{3-2x}{\pi}\right)^2+x^2 \\ &=\dfrac{(3-2x)^2}{\pi}+x^2 \end{aligned}$$
Differentiating:

The length of string for the square is
$$4x=\dfrac{24}{4+\pi}$$
The length for the circle is
$$6-\dfrac{24}{4+\pi}=\dfrac{6\pi}{4+\pi}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{square: }\dfrac{24}{4+\pi},\quad\text{circle: }\dfrac{6\pi}{4+\pi}$$

Integrate the acceleration:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-e^{-t}-\dfrac12e^{-2t}+c_1$$
Initially $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac32$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac32&=-e^0-\dfrac12e^0+c_1\\ c_1&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dx}{dt}=-e^{-t}-\dfrac12e^{-2t}$$
Integrate again:
$$x=e^{-t}+\dfrac14e^{-2t}+c_2$$
Initially $x=\dfrac34$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac34&=e^0+\dfrac14e^0+c_2\\ c_2&=-\dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=e^{-t}+\dfrac14e^{-2t}-\dfrac12$$

As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-t}\to0$ and $e^{-2t}\to0$.

A number of fish species are subject to minimum length regulations when they are caught.

ie. fish shorter than a given length must be returned to the water if caught.

Two such species are Red Snapper and Barramundi which have minimum lengths of 30 cm and 55 cm respectively.

A fishing tour operator in Northern Australia has made observations over a long period of time and found that, when measured in cm, both the variables ‘R’ (the lengths of caught Red Snapper) and ‘B’ (the lengths of caught Barramundi), are normally distributed.

‘R’ has a mean of 36 cm and standard deviation of 3 cm. ‘B’ has a standard deviation of 4 cm.

parts.latex: Calculate the mean length of Barramundi caught if $2.5\%$ of Barramundi caught are less than 54 cm.

Calculate the $z$-scores for the minimum allowed lengths for both variables, R and B, and comment upon what this means in terms of which of the two species are more likely to be returned to the water after capture.

solutions.latex:
By the empirical rule, $95\%$ of Barramundi are within $2$ standard deviations of the mean, so $5\%$ are more than $2$ standard deviations from the mean.

By symmetry, $2.5\%$ of Barramundi are more than $2$ standard deviations below the mean.

Hence
$$\begin{aligned} 54&=\mu-2s\\ \mu&=54+2\times4\\ &=62\text{ cm} \end{aligned}$$
The mean length of caught Barramundi was $62$ cm.
criteria: Substantial progress towards the correct solution, showing some knowledge of the empirical rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{s}$:

Red Snapper (minimum $30$ cm):
$$z=\dfrac{30-36}{3}=-2$$
Barramundi (minimum $55$ cm, $\mu=62$):
$$z=\dfrac{55-62}{4}=-1.75$$
By the empirical rule, only $2.5\%$ of caught Red Snapper are returned, since the minimum length is $2$ standard deviations below the mean.

The Barramundi minimum is only $1.75$ standard deviations below the mean, so more than $2.5\%$ of Barramundi are returned.

Therefore caught Barramundi are more likely to be returned to the water.
criteria: Correct answer, showing $z$-scores for both species and correct, logical reasoning as to which species is more likely to be returned
Two of the three elements correct (reasoning based on a single incorrect $z$-score is acceptable), or equivalent merit
One of the three elements correct (correct reasoning based on incorrect $z$-scores is acceptable), or equivalent merit

From the table, the $z$-score for being faster than $89.97\%$ of applicants is $1.28$, and for $90.15\%$ it is $1.29$.

The qualifying time (faster means below the mean) is
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\mu-1.28s\\ &=5\text{ minutes}-1.28\times30\text{ seconds}\\ &=4\text{ minutes }21.6\text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
or, using $1.29$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\mu-1.29s\\ &=5\text{ minutes}-1.29\times30\text{ seconds}\\ &=4\text{ minutes }21.3\text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

The gradient of the tangent is $f'(x)$.

$f(x)$ is many-to-one when the cubic has two stationary points, that is, when $f'(x)=0$ has two real roots, so the discriminant of $f'(x)$ is positive.

$$\Delta=b^2-4ac=0+12(m^2-4)$$

Charlie is applying for membership at a new golf club that has a strong reputation. The scores of his current club have a lower quartile of 110 and an upper quartile of 118 and Charlie’s score is not an outlier.

Given that the club he plans to join has scores with a lower quartile of 90 and an upper quartile of 106, can you assure Charlie that his score will not be an outlier in his new club? Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.
parts.note: Quartiles, IQR and outliers are not in 2024 Advanced (Mathematics Standard).

solutions.latex:
A score is an outlier if it lies outside $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$ and $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

Current club:
$$IQR=118-110=8$$
$$1.5\times IQR=12$$
$$\text{Upper bound}=118+12=130,\quad\text{Lower bound}=110-12=98$$
$\therefore$ Charlie's score is between $98$ and $130$.

New club:
$$IQR=106-90=16$$
$$1.5\times IQR=24$$
$$\text{Upper bound}=106+24=130,\quad\text{Lower bound}=90-24=66$$
$\therefore$ Charlie is not an outlier in the new club, as his score is not outside the bounds $66$ to $130$.

4196.stem:
Mani is a fruit grower. After his oranges are picked, they are sorted by a machine, according to size. The distribution of the diameter, in centimetres, of oranges is modelled by a continuous random variable, $X$, with probability density function given below.

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{3x^3}{4}+15x^2-99x+216 & 6\le x\le 8\\[6pt] 0 & \text{Otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ for the domain $6\le x\le 8$.
Hence or otherwise, find the probability that a randomly selected orange has a diameter greater than 7cm.
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

parts.latex: Find the mode of the distribution.

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_6^x f(t)\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned}F(x)&=\int_6^x\left(-\dfrac{3t^3}{4}+15t^2-99t+216\right)dt\\&=\left[-\dfrac{3}{16}t^4+5t^3-\dfrac{99}{2}t^2+216t\right]_6^x\\&=-\dfrac{3}{16}x^4+5x^3-\dfrac{99}{2}x^2+216x-351\end{aligned}$$
criteria: States the integral for $F(x)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Corrected from source: the integrand and the antiderivative bracket had the $t^3$ and $t^4$ terms with a missing minus sign (written $+\dfrac{3t^3}{4}$ and $+\dfrac{3}{16}t^4$). The final $F(x)$ was already right and $F(6)=0$ checks.

solutions.latex:
The mode occurs at the global maximum, that is at a stationary point or at an end of the domain.

End points:
$$f(6)=0,\quad f(8)=0$$
To find stationary points, differentiate:
$$f'(x)=-\dfrac{3}{4}\left(3x^2-40x+132\right)$$
Set $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3x^2-40x+132 &= 0 \\ (3x-22)(x-6) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $x=6$ or $x=\dfrac{22}{3}$.

Values of $f$ at these points:
$$f(6)=0,\quad f\left(\dfrac{22}{3}\right)=\dfrac{8}{9}$$
The greatest value is $\dfrac{8}{9}$, at $x=\dfrac{22}{3}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the mode of the distribution is } \dfrac{22}{3}$$
criteria: Checks the end points, or finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$z=\dfrac{150-134}{16}=1$$
Then

From the table, $P(Z<1.6)=0.945$, and by symmetry $P(Z>-1.6)=0.945$.

Therefore $a$ corresponds to a $z$-score of $-1.6$.
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 134-1.6\times 16 \\ &= 108.4 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $\sin\theta=\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{19}}$ and $\theta$ is obtuse, find the exact value of $\tan\theta$ in simplest form.

solutions.latex:
Since $\theta$ is obtuse, it lies in quadrant 2, so $\sin\theta>0$ and $\tan\theta<0$. Construct a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $2\sqrt{19}$ and opposite side $6+\sqrt{2}$.

\exfigure{1309_q24_s1}

Let $A$ be the adjacent side. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} A^2 &= \left(2\sqrt{19}\right)^2-\left(6+\sqrt{2}\right)^2 \\ &= 76-\left(36+12\sqrt{2}+2\right) \\ &= 76-\left(38+12\sqrt{2}\right) \\ &= 38-12\sqrt{2} \\ &= 36-12\sqrt{2}+2 \\ &= \left(6-\sqrt{2}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$$
so $A=6-\sqrt{2}$.

In quadrant 2 the tangent is negative:
$$\therefore\ \tan\theta=-\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{6-\sqrt{2}}$$
or equivalently
$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{6+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}-6}$$

parts.latex:
Show that the total surface area of the can, $A\text{ cm}^2$, is given by:

$$A=2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right)$$
Find the value of $r$ for which the tin has a minimum surface area.

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cylinder is $V=\pi r^2h$. Given $V=192\pi$:
$$h=\dfrac{192\pi}{\pi r^2}=\dfrac{192}{r^2}\qquad(1)$$
The closed can has two circular ends and a curved surface:
$$A=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh=2\pi\left(r^2+rh\right)\qquad(2)$$
Substitute (1) into (2):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\pi\left(r^2+r\left(\dfrac{192}{r^2}\right)\right) \\ &= 2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes $192\pi$ into the volume formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Write the area with a negative power:
$$A=2\pi\left(r^2+\dfrac{192}{r}\right)=2\pi\left(r^2+192r^{-1}\right)$$
Differentiate:
$$A'=2\pi\left(2r-192r^{-2}\right),\quad A''=2\pi\left(2+384r^{-3}\right)$$
For stationary points, $A'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2r-\dfrac{192}{r^2} &= 0 \\ 2r &= \dfrac{192}{r^2} \\ 2r^3 &= 192 \\ r^3 &= 96 \\ r &= \sqrt[3]{96} \end{aligned}$$
Nature: when $r=\sqrt[3]{96}$,
$$A''=2\pi\left(2+\dfrac{384}{r^3}\right)=2\pi\left(2+\dfrac{384}{96}\right)>0$$
so this is a minimum turning point.
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum surface area occurs when } r=\sqrt[3]{96}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: By solving simultaneously, show that the point of intersection occurs when $x=2$.
Hence, or otherwise, find the shaded area of the region bounded by the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis and the two curves, correct to 4 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
At the intersection the two $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x} &= 2^{-x} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= 2\times 2^{-x} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= 2^{1-x} \\ 2^{-1} &= 2^{1-x} \\ -1 &= 1-x \\ x &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Must solve simultaneously.

solutions.latex:
Find the $x$-intercept of $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x} &= 0 \\ 2^{-1} &= 2^{-x} \\ x &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The shaded area is the area under $y=2^{-x}$ from $0$ to $2$, minus the area under $y=\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}$ from $1$ to $2$:
$$A=\int_0^2 2^{-x}\,dx-\int_1^2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-2^{-x}\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= -\left[\dfrac{2^{-x}}{\ln 2}\right]_0^2-\left[\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{2^{-x}}{\ln 2}\right]_1^2 \\ &= -\left(\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{\ln 2}\right)-\left(\left(\dfrac{2}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4\ln 2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2\ln 2}\right)\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\ln 2}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &\approx 0.9427 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expresses the area using the correct integrals, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Show that

$$\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$$

Hence, solve the equation

$$6\log_x 2+\log_2 x-5=0$$

solutions.latex:
To prove: $\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$.

Using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$, with base $c=b$:
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= \log_a b \\ &= \dfrac{\log_b b}{\log_b a} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\log_b a} \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Must use proper setting out for a proof.

solutions.latex:
By part (a), $\log_x 2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2 x}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 6\log_x 2+\log_2 x-5 &= 0 \\ \dfrac{6}{\log_2 x}+\log_2 x-5 &= 0 \\ 6+(\log_2 x)^2-5\log_2 x &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $u=\log_2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u^2-5u+6 &= 0 \\ (u-3)(u-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $u=3$ or $u=2$.

For $\log_2 x=3$: $x=2^3=8$.

For $\log_2 x=2$: $x=2^2=4$.
$$\therefore\ x=4 \text{ or } x=8$$
criteria: Forms the quadratic, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A weight is attached to a spring that is connected to the ceiling. The weight is pulled away from the ceiling and then released so that it bounces up and down.

Let the distance of the weight from the ceiling be $x$ metres. The spring stretches and contracts such that $x$ varies sinusoidally with time, between 1.2 metres and 1.8 metres. It takes 1 second for the weight to go from its highest point to its lowest point.

The motion of the weight can be modelled using a sine wave of the form:

$$x=a\sin(bt+c)+d$$

How far from the ceiling is the weight 2.7 seconds after it is at a high point?

solutions.latex:
Since $x$ is the distance from the ceiling, the high point is at $x=1.2$ and the low point is at $x=1.8$.

Amplitude and centre of motion:
$$a=\dfrac{1.8-1.2}{2}=0.3,\qquad d=\dfrac{1.8+1.2}{2}=1.5$$
The time from high to low is 1 s, which is half a period:
$$\text{period}=2\times 1=\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$$
so $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$.

Assuming the weight starts ($t=0$) at the centre of motion, the distance from the ceiling is modelled by
$$x=0.3\sin(\pi t)+1.5$$
The weight is at a high point when $x=1.2$, that is when $\sin(\pi t)=-1$, which first occurs at $t=1.5$.

The required time is 2.7 s after this:
$$1.5+2.7=4.2$$
When $t=4.2$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 0.3\sin(\pi\times 4.2)+1.5 \\ &\approx 1.676 \text{ m (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$
As the period is 2, the same answer follows from $t=1.5+0.7$, that is $t=0.2$.
criteria: Substitutes the correct time to find $x$, with one error, or equivalent merit
Finds $t=1.5$ for the highest point (or equivalent), or equivalent merit
Finds $b=\pi$ and recognises that the highest point corresponds to $x=1.2$, or equivalent merit

4211.stem:
A competition is run where 400 raffle tickets are placed in a box.

There are two prizes to be won. The ticket for first prize is drawn from the box without replacement, and then the ticket for second prize is drawn from the box.

Rex has 20 tickets in the raffle. Find the probability that he wins:

parts.latex: no prizes.
at least one prize.

solutions.latex:
Rex has 20 of the 400 tickets, so 380 tickets are not his. Without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{no prizes}) &= \dfrac{380}{400} \times \dfrac{379}{399} \\ &= \dfrac{379}{420} \\ &\approx 90.2\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

Use the complement of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one prize}) &= 1 - \dfrac{379}{420} \\ &= \dfrac{41}{420} \\ &\approx 9.8\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A Lotto game is conducted where 5 balls are selected without replacement from 50 balls, which are numbered from 1 to 50.

A Lotto game is conducted and all five balls are drawn.

Find the probability that all of the balls drawn have even numbers.

solutions.latex:
There are 25 even numbers among the 50 balls. Without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{25}{50} \times \dfrac{24}{49} \times \dfrac{23}{48} \times \dfrac{22}{47} \times \dfrac{21}{46} \\ &= \dfrac{33}{1316} \\ &\approx 2.5\% \text{ (to 1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: For two events $X$ and $Y$, find $P(X \mid Y)$ if $P(X \cap Y) = 0.3$ and $P(Y) = 0.4$

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(X \mid Y) &= \dfrac{P(X \cap Y)}{P(Y)} \\ &= \dfrac{0.3}{0.4} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4} \text{ or } 75\% \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: Venn diagram of overlapping events A and B

solutions.latex:
Using the complement and the addition formula:
$$\begin{aligned} P(\overline{A \cup B}) &= 1 - P(A \cup B) \\ &= 1 - \left[P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\right] \\ &= 1 - \left[\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right] \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{11}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the addition formula, or equivalent merit

Jason borrows $\$400\,000$ at $7.2\%$ p.a. The interest is compounded monthly on the amount owing. The terms of the loan are that no repayments are made for one year and then equal monthly repayments of $\$M$ are made for another 9 years. Hence the terms of the loan are for 10 years in total.

The monthly rate is $\dfrac{7.2\%}{12} = 0.6\%$, so each month multiplies by $1.006$.

No repayments are made for the first 12 months:
$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 400000 \times 1.006 \\ A_2 &= 400000 \times 1.006^2 \\ &\ \vdots \\ A_{12} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{12} \end{aligned}$$
The first repayment is at the end of month 13:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{13} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{13} - M \\ A_{14} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{14} - 1.006M - M \\ A_{15} &= 400000 \times 1.006^{15} - 1.006^2M - 1.006M - M \\ &= 400000 \times 1.006^{15} - M\left(1 + 1.006 + 1.006^2\right) \end{aligned}$$

Following the pattern of part (a), after $n$ months:
$$A_n = 400000 \times 1.006^n - M\left(1 + 1.006 + 1.006^2 + \cdots + 1.006^{n-13}\right)$$
So for $n = 120$:
$$A_{120} = 400000 \times 1.006^{120} - M\left(1 + 1.006 + \cdots + 1.006^{107}\right)$$

$$0 = 400000 \times 1.006^{120} - M\left(\dfrac{1.006^{108} - 1}{0.006}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 400000 \times 1.006^{120} \times \dfrac{0.006}{1.006^{108} - 1} \\ &= \$5418.46 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the stationary points on the curve $y=f(x)$ and determine their nature.
Sketch the graph, showing clearly the stationary points and any axis intercepts.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $f(x)=4x^3-x^4$:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=12x^2-4x^3\\ &=4x^2(3-x)\end{aligned}$$

Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

$$f(0)=0,\qquad f(3)=4(27)-81=27$$

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(3,27)$.

Nature: the second derivative is

$$f''(x)=24x-12x^2=12x(2-x)$$

At $x=3$: $f''(3)=12(3)(-1)=-36<0$, so $(3,27)$ is a local maximum.

At $x=0$: $f''(0)=0$, so the test is inconclusive and we test the sign of $f'(x)=4x^2(3-x)$ either side.

$$\begin{aligned} f'(-1)&=4(1)(4)=16>0\\ f'(1)&=4(1)(2)=8>0\end{aligned}$$

The gradient is positive on both sides of $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

$$\therefore\ (3,27)\text{ is a local maximum and }(0,0)\text{ is a horizontal point of inflection}$$

Swimming takes $5\sqrt{5}$ minutes per km, so the swimming time is $5\sqrt{5}\left(\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)$ minutes.

The running distance is $QY=PY-PQ=(2-x)$ km, at $5$ minutes per km, so the running time is $5(2-x)$ minutes.

parts.latex: Find the $x$ value of the maximum turning point on the curve $f(x)=\cos x-\sin x$ between $[0,2\pi]$.

solutions.latex:
Turning points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$f'(x) = -\sin x - \cos x$$
$$\begin{aligned} -\sin x - \cos x &= 0 \\ \tan x &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
For $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, $\tan x = -1$ gives $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ or $x = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$.

The second derivative decides the nature of each point.
$$f''(x) = -\cos x + \sin x$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \sqrt{2} > 0 &&\text{minimum}\\ f''\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = -\sqrt{2} < 0 &&\text{maximum} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Solves $f'(x)=0$ for both values of $x$, or equivalent merit

A particle moves in a straight line.

Its velocity $v$ ms$^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=\dfrac{6}{t+1}-3$

Find the exact distance travelled by the particle in the first 5 seconds.

(answer to 2 decimal places).

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{6}{t+1} - 3 &= 0 \\ t + 1 &= 2 \\ t &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, with $v = 6(t+1)^{-1} - 3$.
$$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -\dfrac{6}{(t+1)^2}$$
When $t=1$:
$$a = -\dfrac{6}{4} = -\dfrac{3}{2}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the acceleration is } -\dfrac{3}{2} \text{ ms}^{-2}$$
criteria: Finds $t=1$ when stationary, or finds $a=-\dfrac{6}{(t+1)^2}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Intercepts and asymptote:
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:\ v &= 6 - 3 = 3 \\ v=0:\ t &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
As $t \to \infty$, $\dfrac{6}{t+1} \to 0$, so $v \to -3$: the horizontal asymptote is $v=-3$.

criteria: Finds the intercepts or the asymptote, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From the graph, $v \ge 0$ for $0 \le t \le 1$ and $v < 0$ for $1 < t \le 5$. The particle turns round at $t=1$, so the two stages are found separately.

An antiderivative of $v$ is
$$x = 6\ln(t+1) - 3t$$
Distance in the first second:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 v\,dt &= \big[6\ln(t+1) - 3t\big]_0^1 \\ &= (6\ln 2 - 3) - 0 \\ &= 6\ln 2 - 3 \end{aligned}$$
Displacement from $t=1$ to $t=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5 v\,dt &= (6\ln 6 - 15) - (6\ln 2 - 3) \\ &= 6\ln 3 - 12 \end{aligned}$$
This is negative ($\approx -5.41$), so the distance in this stage is $12 - 6\ln 3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total distance} &= (6\ln 2 - 3) + (12 - 6\ln 3) \\ &= 9 + 6\ln 2 - 6\ln 3 \\ &= 9 - 6\ln\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance} = 9 - 6\ln\dfrac{3}{2} \approx 6.57 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Integrates $v$ correctly and evaluates both stages, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total is 80 and 12 people did not holiday, so $80 - 12 = 68$ people holidayed.

Both: $42 + 36 - 68 = 10$.

solutions.latex:
Ten people holidayed both interstate and within NSW.
$$P(\text{I}\cap\text{N}) = \dfrac{10}{80} = \dfrac18$$

Of the 80 people, $80 - 12 = 68$ have travelled, and 36 of them holidayed within NSW.
$$P(\text{N}\mid\text{traveller}) = \dfrac{36}{68} = \dfrac{9}{17}$$

$42$ people went interstate, so $80-42 = 38$ did not. Exactly one interstate traveller means the order is (I, not I) or (not I, I), without replacement.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly one I}) &= P(\text{I},\overline{\text{I}}) + P(\overline{\text{I}},\text{I}) \\ &= \dfrac{42}{80}\times\dfrac{38}{79} + \dfrac{38}{80}\times\dfrac{42}{79} \\ &= \dfrac{399}{790} \end{aligned}$$

4277.stem: A particle, initially at the origin, is moving in a straight line. Its velocity, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, after $t$ seconds is given by $v = 2 - 2t$.

parts.latex: Find the initial velocity.
Find when the particle is at rest.
Find when the particle is next at the origin.
Find the distance travelled in the first 4 seconds.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 0$ into $v = 2 - 2t$.
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 2 - 2(0) \\ &= 2 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2-2t \\ 2t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 1 \text{ second}$$

Position is the integral of velocity, so $x=\displaystyle\int v\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int (2-2t)\,dt \\ &= 2t - t^2 + C \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$, giving $C=0$.
$$x = 2t - t^2$$
The particle is at the origin when $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2t - t^2 \\ &= t(2-t) \end{aligned}$$
So $t=0$ or $t=2$. The particle is next at the origin when $t\ne 0$.
$$\therefore\ t = 2 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Correct answer (student must evaluate the constant of integration)
Demonstrates an understanding that $x=\displaystyle\int v\,dt$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when it comes to rest, at $t=1$, so find $x$ at $t=0$, $1$ and $4$ using $x=2t-t^2$.

When $t=0$, $x=0$ (given in the initial conditions).

When $t=1$:
$$x = 2(1)-1^2 = 1$$
When $t=4$:
$$x = 2(4)-4^2 = -8$$
So the particle starts at the origin, moves right to $x=1$ and then travels left to $x=-8$.

Distance travelled:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 1 + (1+8) \\ &= 10 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle travels a total of } 10 \text{ m in the first 4 seconds}$$
criteria: Finds $x$ when $t=1$, or finds $x$ when $t=4$, or states the particle has travelled 8 m, or uses integration to arrive at an answer of 8 m, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$.

solutions.latex:
The probabilities in a distribution sum to 1.
$$\dfrac{32}{243}+k+k+\dfrac{40}{243}+\dfrac{10}{243}+\dfrac{1}{243}=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2k+\dfrac{83}{243} &= 1 \\ 2k &= \dfrac{160}{243} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{80}{243}$$

solutions.latex:
Using $\mathrm{E}(X)=\sum x\,P(X=x)$ and $k=\dfrac{80}{243}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}(X) &= 0\left(\dfrac{32}{243}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+2\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+3\left(\dfrac{40}{243}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{10}{243}\right)+5\left(\dfrac{1}{243}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{405}{243} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{3} \end{aligned}$$

Using $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathrm{E}(X^2)-\mu^2$ with $\mu=\dfrac{5}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(X) &= \left[0\left(\dfrac{32}{243}\right)+1\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+4\left(\dfrac{80}{243}\right)+9\left(\dfrac{40}{243}\right)+16\left(\dfrac{10}{243}\right)+25\left(\dfrac{1}{243}\right)\right]-\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{10}{9} \end{aligned}$$
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
$$\therefore\ \sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{9}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{3}$$

4280.stem: The function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{6} - \dfrac{x^2}{4} - 3x + 1$ is defined for $x$ in the domain $[-4, 6]$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of f(x) with stationary points and endpoints

parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
Find the absolute maximum of $f(x)$.
Sketch $f(x)$ showing the stationary points and both endpoints.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the stationary points.
$$f'(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}-3$$
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \dfrac{x^2}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}-3 \\ 0 &= x^2-x-6 \\ &= (x-3)(x+2) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-2$ or $x=3$.

The $y$ values:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-2) &= \dfrac{(-2)^3}{6}-\dfrac{(-2)^2}{4}-3(-2)+1 \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{3}-1+6+1 \\ &= 4\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(3) &= \dfrac{3^3}{6}-\dfrac{3^2}{4}-3(3)+1 \\ &= \dfrac{27}{6}-\dfrac{9}{4}-9+1 \\ &= -5\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$
Use the second derivative to determine the nature.
$$f''(x)=x-\dfrac{1}{2}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f''(-2) &= -2-\dfrac{1}{2}=-2\dfrac{1}{2}<0 \\ f''(3) &= 3-\dfrac{1}{2}=2\dfrac{1}{2}>0 \end{aligned}$$
So there is a local maximum at $\left(-2,\,4\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ and a local minimum at $\left(3,\,-5\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$.
criteria: Correct answer (values of $f''(-2)$ and $f''(3)$ must be given to determine nature; if a table of values is used, numerical values of $f'(x)$ must be given)
Correct derivative and finds both stationary points, including the $y$ values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The absolute maximum on $[-4,6]$ is the greatest of the local maximum and the endpoint values. The local maximum is $4\dfrac{2}{3}$, so evaluate the endpoints.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-4) &= \dfrac{(-4)^3}{6}-\dfrac{(-4)^2}{4}-3(-4)+1 \\ &= -10\dfrac{2}{3}-4+12+1 \\ &= -1\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f(6) &= \dfrac{6^3}{6}-\dfrac{6^2}{4}-3(6)+1 \\ &= 36-9-18+1 \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the absolute maximum of } f(x) \text{ is } 10$$
criteria: Calculates either $f(-4)$ or $f(6)$, or equivalent merit

4282.stem: The percentage results of a university entrance examination are normally distributed with a mean mark is 60 and the standard deviation is 8.

figures.cap: normal curve with area shaded between Zoe and Tyler

parts.latex: If Jimmy's mark corresponds to a negative $z$-score in the range, $-1 < z < 0$ give a possible value for Jimmy's mark.
Tyler obtains a result of $72\%$. Show that his $z$-score is 1.5.
Zoe's $z$-score was 1. What was her percentage mark?

solutions.latex:
Here $\mu=60$ and $\sigma=8$. A $z$-score between $-1$ and $0$ means the mark lies between $\mu-\sigma=52$ and $\mu=60$.

Any mark in the range $52<x<60$ is possible, for example $56$.

meta.source_flag: The source answer is 'any integer in the range $56<x<64$', but $-1<z<0$ with $\mu=60$, $\sigma=8$ gives $52<x<60$; marks from $60$ to $64$ have $z\ge 0$. The range in my working replaces the source range.
meta.format_note: Corrected from source: range $56<x<64$ replaced by $52<x<60$ (derived from $z=\dfrac{x-60}{8}$). Original source text: 'Any integer in the range $56 < x < 64$.'

solutions.latex:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{72-60}{8} \\ &= 1.5 \end{aligned}$$
as required.

Rearranging the $z$-score formula, $x=\mu+z\sigma$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 60+1(8) \\ &= 68 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Zoe's mark was } 68\%$$

By the empirical rule, a $z$-score of 1 means Zoe's result is better than $50\%+34\%=84\%$ of scores.

Tyler's result is better than $93.3\%$ of scores, so the percentage between Zoe and Tyler is
$$93.3\%-84\%=9.3\%$$
Students represented by the shaded region:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 9.3\%\times 85000 \\ &= 7905 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Indicates that Zoe's mark is better than $84\%$ of scores, or equivalent merit

4283.stem:
$X$ is a continuous random variable that is defined by the probability density function,

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} k(x-1)^2 & 2 \le x \le 4 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Show that $k = \dfrac{3}{26}$.
Find the cumulative distribution function.
Show that the upper quartile is approximately 3.74.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function, the total area is 1.
$$\int_2^4 k(x-1)^2\,dx = 1$$
$$\begin{aligned} \left[\dfrac{k(x-1)^3}{3}\right]_2^4 &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k(4-1)^3}{3}-\dfrac{k(2-1)^3}{3} &= 1 \\ \dfrac{k}{3}\left(3^3-1^3\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{26k}{3} &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{3}{26}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct answer with adequate working given it is a show that question
Sets the integral of the PDF equal to 1, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is the integral of the PDF from the lower limit, with $k=\dfrac{3}{26}$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_2^x \dfrac{3}{26}(x-1)^2\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{26}\right]_2^x \\ &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3}{26}-\dfrac{1}{26} \\ &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3-1}{26} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integration of the PDF, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric 'one mark for each line with a tick' rewritten by us as a top-down rubric. Source uses $x$ as both the limit and the variable of integration, and gives the CDF only for $2\le x\le 4$; kept as in source.

solutions.latex:
The upper quartile is the value of $x$ where the CDF equals $0.75$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.75 &= \dfrac{(x-1)^3-1}{26} \\ 19.5 &= (x-1)^3-1 \\ 20.5 &= (x-1)^3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x-1 &= \sqrt[3]{20.5} \\ x &= \sqrt[3]{20.5}+1 \\ &\approx 3.736851837 \\ &\approx 3.74 \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct answer with adequate working given it is a show that question
Sets the CDF equal to $0.75$, or equivalent merit

4284.stem:
An iron has accidently been left on. Fortunately, it switches itself off after a period of time.

The temperature of the iron can be modelled by the equation,

$$T = 22 + 162(1.2)^{-0.5t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the iron's surface, in degrees Celsius, $t$ minutes after the iron switches itself off.

parts.latex: What is the temperature of the iron 6 minutes after it has switched off ? Give your answer to the nearest degree.
At what rate is the temperature of the iron's surface changing after 6 minutes ?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=6$ into the model.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 22+162(1.2)^{-0.5(6)} \\ &\approx 116^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric row was 'substitution of 6 for $t$'; changed to 'Correct answer' as the single full-mark row.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{u}\right)=a^{u}\ln a\cdot u'$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= 162(-0.5)(1.2)^{-0.5t}(\ln 1.2) \\ &= -81(1.2)^{-0.5t}(\ln 1.2) \end{aligned}$$
When $t=6$:
$$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-81(1.2)^{-0.5(6)}(\ln 1.2)\approx -8.5^\circ\text{C per minute}$$

meta.marker_note: 1 mark if the student omits $\ln 1.2$ from the derivative but completes the question correctly (they will get $-46.875^\circ$C per minute).

parts.latex: Find the area of the $10^{\text{th}}$ annulus.
Show that the sum of the first $n$ annuli is found by $S_n = \pi n^2 + 2n\pi$
What is the minimum number of annuli needed for a combined area of $300\ \text{u}^2$ ?

solutions.latex:
The areas of the annuli moving outwards form the arithmetic sequence $3\pi,\ 5\pi,\ 7\pi,\ \ldots$ with $a=3\pi$ and $d=2\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_n &= a+(n-1)d \\ T_{10} &= 3\pi+(10-1)2\pi \\ &= 21\pi \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area of the } 10^{\text{th}} \text{ annulus is } 21\pi \text{ square units}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; wrote a one-row rubric ('Correct answer', 1 mark) from the question's mark allocation.

solutions.latex:
The sum of $n$ terms of an arithmetic series is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2a+(n-1)d\right]$, with $a=3\pi$ and $d=2\pi$.
$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(3\pi)+(n-1)2\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[3\pi+(n-1)\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[3\pi+n\pi-\pi\right] \\ &= n\left[n\pi+2\pi\right] \\ &= \pi n^2+2n\pi \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correct answer with adequate working given it is a show that question
Substitutes $a=3\pi$ and $d=2\pi$ into the sum formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us from the mark allocation (2 marks).

solutions.latex:
We need the combined area to be at least $300$.
$$\pi n^2+2n\pi\ge 300$$
$$\pi n^2+2n\pi-300\ge 0$$
Solve $\pi n^2+2n\pi-300=0$ using the quadratic formula.
$$n=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}=\dfrac{-2\pi\pm\sqrt{4\pi^2+1200\pi}}{2\pi}$$
Since $n>0$, only the positive root applies.
$$n=\dfrac{-2\pi+\sqrt{4\pi^2+1200\pi}}{2\pi}\approx 8.8$$
The quadratic $f(n)=\pi n^2+2n\pi-300$ is an upward parabola, so $f(n)\ge 0$ for $n\ge 8.8$. Since $n$ is a whole number, the minimum is $n=9$.
$$\therefore\ 9 \text{ annuli are required for a total area of } 300 \text{ u}^2$$

4286.stem:
Nick chooses an integer, $x$, between 1 and 20 at random.

He reduces this number by 1, 4 and 9 in turn and then multiplies to find the product, $P$.

parts.latex: Show that, $P = x^3 - 14x^2 + 49x - 36$
Find the minimum value of $P$.

solutions.latex:
Reducing $x$ by 1, 4 and 9 gives the factors, so $P=(x-1)(x-4)(x-9)$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= (x-1)(x^2-13x+36) \\ &= x^3-13x^2+36x-x^2+13x-36 \\ &= x^3-14x^2+49x-36 \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.format_note: Source rubric row was 'establishment of the result through expansion'; changed to 'Correct answer' as the single full-mark row.

solutions.latex:
Minimum values occur where $P'(x)=0$.
$$P'(x)=3x^2-28x+49$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 3x^2-28x+49 \\ &= (3x-7)(x-7) \end{aligned}$$
So $x=\dfrac{7}{3}$ or $x=7$. Since $x$ is an integer, $x=7$ only.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$P''(x)=6x-28$$
When $x=7$, $P''=14>0$, so $x=7$ gives a minimum.

The minimum value:
$$\begin{aligned} P(7) &= (7-1)(7-4)(7-9) \\ &= -36 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum value of } P \text{ is } -36$$
criteria: $x=7$ and establishes that this value minimises $P$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Jelena retires with a balance in her superannuation account of \$700 000.

The fund earns interest at the rate of $3.6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly.

At the end of each month, Jelena withdraws \$4000 from the account.

The amount, $A_n$, left in her fund after the $n^{th}$ withdrawal is given by,

$$A_n = 700000(1.003)^n - 4000\left\{1 + 1.003 + (1.003)^2 + \ldots + (1.003)^{n-1}\right\}$$

(Do NOT prove this result)

Find, correct to the nearest month, the time taken for the balance in the fund to reduce to \$400 000.

solutions.latex:
The balance is to reduce to $\$400\,000$. The bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.003$ and $n$ terms, so its sum is $\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}$.
$$400000=700000(1.003)^n-4000\left(\dfrac{1.003^n-1}{0.003}\right)$$
Multiply both sides by $0.003$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1200 &= 2100(1.003)^n-4000\left(1.003^n-1\right) \\ &= 4000-1900(1.003)^n \end{aligned}$$
$$1.003^n=\dfrac{28}{19}$$
Take logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} n &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{28}{19}\right)}{\ln 1.003} \\ &\approx 129.448963 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ n\approx 129 \text{ months}$$
criteria: $1.003^n=\dfrac{28}{19}$ (accept decimal equivalent on RHS), or equivalent merit
Successful use of the sum to $n$ terms of a GP formula

The diagram below shows the graph of $y = \ln x$. The region bounded by the graph, the $x$-axis and the line $x = 7$ has been shaded.

parts.latex: Use the trapezoidal rule with 3 function values to approximate the shaded area. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x \ln x)$.

Hence, find an approximation for $\ln 7$.

solutions.latex:
With 3 function values the strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{7-1}{2}=3$$
so the $x$ values are $1$, $4$ and $7$. By the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{3}{2}\left[\ln 1+2(\ln 4)+\ln 7\right] \\ &\approx 7.078 \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x) &= x\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)+\ln x\,(1) \\ &= 1+\ln x \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
From (b), $x\ln x$ is an antiderivative of $1+\ln x$.
$$\int_1^7(1+\ln x)\,dx=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7$$
$$\int_1^7 1\,dx+\int_1^7\ln x\,dx=\Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7$$
Rearranging:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^7\ln x\,dx &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\int_1^7 1\,dx \\ &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^7-\Big[x\Big]_1^7 \\ &= (7\ln 7-0)-(7-1) \\ &= 7\ln 7-6 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Given that $f(x)$ is an even function and $g(x)$ is an odd function, which of the following statements is true?

solutions.latex:
Let $h(x) = f[g(x)]$. Since $g$ is odd and $f$ is even:
$$\begin{aligned} h(-x) &= f[g(-x)] \\ &= f[-g(x)] \\ &= f[g(x)] \\ &= h(x) \end{aligned}$$
So $f[g(x)]$ is even.

A fails: for $h(x)=f(x)\times g(x)$, $h(-x) = f(x)\times(-g(x)) = -h(x)$, so it is odd.

B fails: for $h(x)=f(x)+g(x)$, $h(-x) = f(x)-g(x)$, which is neither $h(x)$ nor $-h(x)$.

D fails: for $h(x)=g[f(x)]$, $h(-x)=g[f(x)] = h(x)$, so it is even.

Hence the answer is C.

Show that the particle comes to rest again when it is 12 m to the right of the origin and $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ s.
By finding a function for acceleration, describe the motion of the particle after $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ s and before it next comes to rest.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 8\cos\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)dt \\ &= 8\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right]+C \\ &= 4\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=4$:
$$4=4\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+C=-4+C$$
so $C=8$.
$$\therefore\ x=4\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+8$$
criteria: Correctly finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Method 1: the particle is at rest when $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$\cos\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$$
so $2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ldots$, giving $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\pi,\ldots$

Hence the particle next comes to rest at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds.

Method 2: when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=8\cos\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$x=4\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+8=12 \text{ m}$$
Therefore, at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ the particle is at rest 12 m to the right of the origin.
criteria: Attempts to solve the trigonometric equation $\cos\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$, or equivalent merit

Differentiating the velocity:
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-16\sin\left(2t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$$
When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-16\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=-16$$
The acceleration is negative, so the particle moves towards the left after being stationary at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

4316.stem:
The mass of two substances, $A$ and $B$, are decaying exponentially according to

$$M_A = 200e^{-0.05t}$$
$$M_B = 400 \times 3^{-0.12t},$$

where $M$ is the mass in grams and $t$ is the time in minutes.

parts.latex: Find the time taken for substance $A$ to decrease to half of its original value. Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.
At what instance do both particles decay at the same rate? Give your answer correct to the nearest second.

solutions.latex:
Half the original mass is $M_A=100$:
$$100=200e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\dfrac{1}{2}=e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=-0.05t$$
$$\ln2=0.05t$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln2}{0.05} \\ &= 13.86\ldots \\ &\approx 14 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly arrives at the expression $100=200e^{-0.05t}$ and attempts to solve for $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating each mass:
$$\dfrac{dM_A}{dt}=-0.05\times200e^{-0.05t}=-10e^{-0.05t}$$
$$\dfrac{dM_B}{dt}=400\times\ln3\times(-0.12)\times3^{-0.12t}=-48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$$
Equate the two rates:
$$-10e^{-0.05t}=-48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$$
Write both sides with base $e$, using $3^{-0.12t}=e^{(-0.12\ln3)t}$:
$$\dfrac{10}{48\ln3}=\dfrac{3^{-0.12t}}{e^{-0.05t}}=\dfrac{e^{(-0.12\ln3)t}}{e^{-0.05t}}=e^{(-0.12\ln3+0.05)t}$$
$$0.1895\ldots=e^{-0.0818\ldots t}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\ln0.1895\ldots}{-0.0818\ldots} \\ &= 20.317\ldots \text{ minutes} \\ &\approx 20 \text{ minutes } 19 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Therefore both substances decay at the same rate at 20 minutes and 19 seconds.
criteria: Writes an expression using the same base, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Point $A$ lies on both $y=4-3x^2$ and $y=-x$:
$$4-3x^2=-x$$
$$3x^2-x-4=0$$
$$(3x-4)(x+1)=0$$
so $x=\dfrac{4}{3}$ or $x=-1$. From the diagram $x=-1$, and then $y=4-3(-1)^2=1$.

So $A(-1,1)$ and, by symmetry, $C(1,1)$.

The area of $ABC$ is the area under the curve less the rectangle of height 1 and width 2:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{ABC} &= \int_{-1}^{1}(4-3x^2)\,dx-A_{\text{rectangle}} \\ &= \left[4x-x^3\right]_{-1}^{1}-2 \\ &= (4-1)-(-4+1)-2 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
The logo is four copies of $ABC$ plus two rectangles:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{logo}} &= 4\times A_{ABC}+2\times A_{\text{rectangle}} \\ &= 20 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

4318.stem:
Jonathan's parents decide to set up an investment account to help pay for his university degree. Jonathan's parents deposit \$1000 into the account every year, which earns interest at 4% per annum, compounded yearly. They deposited the first \$1000 at the beginning of the year when Jonathan is born. Jonathan will receive the full amount at the end of the year he turns 18 years old.

Let $A_n$ be the value of the account after $n$ years.

parts.latex:
The amount in the account continues to earn interest at 4% per annum. Jonathan enrols in a four-year university course, which costs $\$M$ each year, to be paid at the end of the year. As a result:

$$A_{19} = 26000\left(1.04^{18} - 1\right)(1.04) - M.$$

How much can Jonathan withdraw from the account each year if the entire amount is to be withdrawn over the four years?

criteria: Correctly finds an unsimplified expression for $A_{18}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Each year the balance grows by $1.04$ and then $M$ is withdrawn:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{20} &= \left[26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)-M\right](1.04)-M \\ &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^2-M(1+1.04) \end{aligned}$$
$$A_{21}=26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^3-M\left(1+1.04+1.04^2\right)$$
By the pattern, using the geometric series sum $\dfrac{1.04^4-1}{0.04}=25\left(1.04^4-1\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} A_{22} &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4-M\left(1+1.04+1.04^2+1.04^3\right) \\ &= 26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4-25M\left(1.04^4-1\right) \end{aligned}$$
The account is empty when $A_{22}=0$:
$$M=\dfrac{26000\left(1.04^{18}-1\right)(1.04)^4}{25\left(1.04^4-1\right)}$$
$$\therefore\ M=\$7347.66$$

parts.latex: Show that the equation $-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 4x + 4\cos 4x = 0$ can be written as $\tan 4x = 8$.

Show that the exact value to the first two solutions to the equation $\tan 4x = 8$ in the domain $[0, \pi]$ are

$$x_1 = \dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8$$

$$\text{and } x_2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi + \tan^{-1}8\right).$$
Write down the $x$-coordinates of $P_1$ and $P_2$.

It is known that the $y$-coordinates of the stationary points $Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, \ldots, Y_n$ form a geometric sequence.

Find the exact value of the common ratio for this geometric sequence. Express your answer in simplest form.
can_use: Testing for arithmetic and geometric sequences

solutions.latex:
Rearranging:
$$4\cos4x=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x$$
$$8\cos4x=\sin4x$$
Dividing both sides by $\cos4x$:
$$\tan4x=8$$

The solutions of $\tan4x=8$ with $0\le4x\le4\pi$ are
$$4x=\tan^{-1}8,\ \pi+\tan^{-1}8,\ 2\pi+\tan^{-1}8$$
so
$$x=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8,\ \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right),\ \dfrac{1}{4}\left(2\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
Therefore the first two solutions are
$$x_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8 \quad\text{and}\quad x_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
criteria: Correctly shows ONE solution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote the range as $[0,4\pi]$ for $4x$ (domain $[0,\pi]$ for $x$); kept.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $y=10e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}\sin4x$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{-\frac{1}{2}x} & v&=\sin4x\\ u'&=-\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{1}{2}x} & v'&=4\cos4x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 10\left[\sin4x\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}+e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}\times4\cos4x\right] \\ &= 10e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x+4\cos4x\right) \end{aligned}$$
For stationary points $y'=0$. Since $e^{-\frac{1}{2}x}>0$, we need $-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x+4\cos4x=0$, which is $\tan4x=8$ by part (a).

Therefore:
$$X_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8,\qquad X_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
criteria: Finds the derivative of $y$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At $X_1=\dfrac{1}{4}\tan^{-1}8$:
$$Y_1=10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\tan^{-1}8}\sin\left(\tan^{-1}8\right)$$
At $X_2=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$, using $\sin(\pi+\theta)=-\sin\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} Y_2 &= 10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)}\sin\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right) \\ &= -10e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)}\sin\left(\tan^{-1}8\right) \end{aligned}$$
The common ratio is
$$\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{Y_2}{Y_1} \\ &= -e^{-\frac{1}{8}\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)+\frac{1}{8}\tan^{-1}8} \\ &= -e^{-\frac{1}{8}\pi} \end{aligned}$$
